Identity/edition note: the title and all 16 author identities match the catalog, but the PDF orders Karl Pertsch before Oier Mees. Its footer says CoRL 2024; the supplied catalog identifies proceedings publication in 2025. No numbered revision or dated revision chain is established; this report identifies the supplied proceedings artifact by its raw PDF hash.

synopsis: SIMPLER builds purpose-specific physics simulations to evaluate real-data-trained manipulation policies. It calibrates action execution and visual observations, then tests whether simulated successes preserve real policy rankings and robustness trends. Its strongest evidence concerns rigid-object tasks on Google Robot and WidowX; useful ranking signals coexist with absolute-success errors and reporting inconsistencies (e02, e10–e13, e23).

problem.text: Real robot evaluation becomes expensive and difficult to standardize as policies cover more tasks. SIMPLER seeks a scalable improvement signal: preserve relative performance without requiring a full-fidelity digital twin or replacing physical evaluation.

contributions.text: An evaluation suite connects pretrained policies to Google Robot and WidowX/BridgeData V2 simulations. Control calibration and visual matching address separate transfer gaps.
MMRV weights ranking mistakes by real performance margins. Paired evaluation and controlled appearance shifts test both model selection and policy-specific robustness.

inputs: A real-data-trained policy, language instruction, RGB observations and applicable proprioception
Offline action/pose trajectories; robot/object assets, camera parameters and real background images
outputs: Executed simulated rollouts and task-success rates
Real/simulation ranking agreement and controlled robustness comparisons

steps.name: Calibrate action effects
steps.detail: Replay identical actions from matched initial poses. Minimize translation and rotation discrepancy by tuning stiffness and damping on 20 existing offline trajectories with different instructions, using three narrowing rounds of simulated annealing.

steps.name: Construct policy observations
steps.detail: Replace the rendered background with a cleaned real image using foreground masks. Align real object images to meshes and transfer textures; tune robot colors. Variant Aggregation instead averages over changed backgrounds, lights, distractors and table textures.

steps.name: Run matched tasks
steps.detail: Match instructions, poses and success criteria. Planned Google trial counts are 75 for can picking, 60 for move-near, 54 for drawers and 27 for drawer-apple; Appendix A lists 24 per WidowX task. Average Google simulations over four arm colors and Octo simulations over three seeds.

steps.name: Score evaluation fidelity
steps.detail: Compare success rates using MMRV and Pearson r. Keep partial grasp success separate from completion, and retain each comparison’s policy roster and task aggregation.

training.text: The main workflow evaluates existing RT-1 checkpoints, RT-1-X, RT-2-X and Octo. Simulator calibration fits parameters; it does not train a joint future/action model. A separate appendix experiment trains RT-1 solely on can-picking demonstrations.

inference.text: The policy receives current observations/instructions and emits translation, rotation and gripper commands. Embodiment-specific controllers apply inverse kinematics and joint targets, yielding new simulated observations. RT-1 uses 3 Hz control/501 Hz simulation; WidowX uses 5/500 Hz. Drawer-apple instructions switch at termination or half the time limit.

equations.explanation: For N policies, R_i and R_{S,i} are real and simulated performance. The indicator selects disagreeing strict comparisons; each policy contributes its largest violated real-performance margin. Lower is better. This measures ranking fidelity, not absolute calibration.

M marks simulated foreground objects and robot pixels; I_sim is the rendering and I_real the cleaned real background. Elementwise compositing preserves simulated interaction geometry while matching the background.

This is the printed loss. Over T steps, x and R denote end-effector positions and rotation matrices; primes denote simulated replay under stiffness p and damping d. The loss adds translation and the displayed rotation discrepancies.

results.task: Google Robot policy ranking: three-task protocol comparison
results.setting: Table 1: six checkpoints across Pick Can, Move Near and Drawer; matched real/sim evaluation.
results.interpretation: Best printed averages favor Visual Matching. These are not success rates; RT-1 MSE samples training data, and Table 10 changes drawer values.

results.setting: Figure 4, Visual Matching; Google tasks and Bridge grasp/completion outcomes.
results.comparison: Real success is the reference, with policy shapes and task colors distinguished.
results.interpretation: Association does not establish equal success probabilities. These summaries differ from Table 1 and the expanded Table 2 roster.

results.task: Pick Coke Can under novel arm textures
results.setting: RT-1-X and Octo-Base; simulated texture variants and real gift-wrapped arms.
results.metric: Real original → OOD success; simulated success range
results.comparison: Real drops are 24.0 and 29.3 percentage points, respectively.
results.interpretation: Simulation anticipates policy-specific sensitivity; its range is not a confidence interval or calibrated real-success prediction.

results.setting: Google Robot Visual Matching with perturbed stiffness/damping.
results.interpretation: Worse replay tracking accompanies worse ranking fidelity; this does not validate all contact dynamics.

results.setting: Section 5.4 component combinations; checkpoint naming conflicts with Table 7.
results.comparison: No components: 0.087 / 0.272; green screen plus drawer-only matching: MMRV 0.142.
results.interpretation: Combined curation helps; adding components is not uniformly beneficial. Text names RT-1 Begin, but Table 7 names RT-1 15%.

results.task: Sensitivity to can mass and gripper friction
results.setting: Table 8(a): six Google policies; masses 10–80 g and friction coefficients 0.25–2.0.
results.interpretation: Ranking tolerates these approximate rigid-body parameters; dexterous and soft-object transfer remains untested.

results.setting: Table 9: five policies, Variant Aggregation, Pick Coke Can and Move Near.
results.comparison: Against paired real success; the paper also reports SAPIEN evaluations.
results.interpretation: This supports portability on a restricted subset, not interchangeable absolute success across simulators.

limitations.text: Rigid-object tasks, RGB/proprioception, fixed-camera green screening, imperfect shadows and manual scene curation limit scope. Preliminary Gaussian-splatting scenes were inadequate; contact-free calibration may fail for fast collisions or dexterity.

Inconsistencies remain: Table 2 adds OpenVLA, Table 10 changes drawer metrics, Table 7 changes an ablation checkpoint, and the augmented robustness plot gives MMRV 0.016 versus Table 4’s 0.041. RT-1 Begin drawer testing stopped after two real trials.

Tables provide point estimates without correlation confidence intervals. Non-significant Kruskal-Wallis tests do not establish equivalence, and favorable pooled correlations can conceal weaker individual tasks.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires exact checkpoints, paired real rollouts, matched cameras/assets and aggregation rules. Preserve Temporal Gauss-Seidel, controller frequencies, Octo seeds and arm-color averaging. The PDF leaves software pins, compute budget, annealing bounds/schedule and absolute episode time limits unspecified.

Proposed checks should separately vary calibration and appearance matching with fixed policies and initial states, measuring ranking and absolute gaps with repeated-trial uncertainty. Resolve the drawer checkpoint mismatch first.

reasoning.text: The recorded benchmark/simulator classification fits a physics-based evaluation suite for existing policies. No learned world/action architecture is proposed for One Model, joint future/action prediction or inverse-dynamics classification; the architecture, paradigm and quadrant are appropriately not applicable.

discussionQuestions: Would ranking fidelity survive a new policy family without retuning textures?
How much paired real evaluation distinguishes simulator bias from uncertain rankings?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author/affiliation block and conference footer
evidence.detail: The title matches the catalog. The 16 authors appear with Karl Pertsch before Oier Mees. Affiliations are UC San Diego, Stanford University, UC Berkeley and Google Deepmind. The footer identifies CoRL 2024, Munich, Germany; no numbered revision is printed.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Figure 2 and Sections 1 and 3, problem formulation
evidence.detail: SIMPLER evaluates policies trained on real data in simulated Google Robot and WidowX/BridgeData V2 environments through a Gym interface. Its target is relative-performance correlation, complementing physical evaluation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 3, Section 3 and Eq. (1)
evidence.detail: MMRV averages each policy’s maximum misranking penalty, weighted by the real-performance margin. Pearson r measures linear association. The figure depicts small/large horizontal real-performance gaps, nonlinear rankings and noise sensitivity.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 4.1, system-identification loss and optimization paragraphs
evidence.detail: Open-loop replay compares real/simulated end-effector positions and rotation matrices under identical actions. Twenty offline trajectories with different instructions and three rounds of simulated annealing tune stiffness and damping without collecting new calibration data.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, unnumbered visual-matching figure and compositing equation
evidence.detail: Real backgrounds with foreground removed are combined with simulated foreground masks. Object textures are projected from aligned real images; tuned arm colors address appearance changes during rollouts.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2 continuation; PDF p. 18, Figure 5 and Appendix B.3
evidence.detail: SIMPLER uses SAPIEN and rigid-object task setups. Variant Aggregation averages over visual variants, with two variations along each of background, lighting, distractors and table texture; it need not visually match reality.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 5.1; PDF pp. 15–16, Appendix A, task lists and averaging protocol
evidence.detail: Paired tests match instructions, poses and success criteria. Planned Google trial counts are 75, 60, 54 and 27 for can, move-near, drawer and drawer-apple tasks; Appendix A lists 24 per WidowX task. Google simulations average four arm colors; Octo simulations average three seeds. Longer tasks switch instructions at termination or half the time limit.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 16–17, Algorithms 1–2 and Appendix B.1
evidence.detail: RT-1 uses 501 Hz simulation and 3 Hz policy control with inverse kinematics and constrained joint trajectory planning; Ruckig is named. WidowX uses 500 Hz simulation and 5 Hz control and retains the previous arm goal. Algorithm 1 filters gripper actions with absolute value below 0.01.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 17–18, Appendix B.2, Robot and Object Assets
evidence.detail: The pipeline uses robot URDFs, camera intrinsics, curated visual/collision meshes and Temporal Gauss-Seidel for Google Robot grasping. Texture alignment uses segmentation, pose adjustment and differentiable rendering; collision meshes use CoACD. Construction remains partly manual.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 1, six-checkpoint caption and MMRV/Pearson r rows
evidence.detail: Across Pick Can, Move Near and Drawer, average MMRV/r are 0.056/0.924 for Visual Matching, 0.143/0.778 for Variant Aggregation and 0.375/0.308 for action MSE. Move Near r favors Variant Aggregation, 0.887 versus 0.855.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 4, both panels and legends
evidence.detail: Figure 4 prints MMRV/r of 0.049/0.929 for Google Robot and 0.014/0.890 for BridgeData V2. Shapes identify policies; colors identify tasks. Bridge includes both grasping and full-task success.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Table 2, policy/metric rows; PDF p. 20, footnotes 2–3
evidence.detail: Table 2 adds OpenVLA-7B to the six policies named in Table 1 and prints different aggregates. RT-1 Begin real drawer testing stopped after two trials due to potential damage. A footnote says continued evaluation could lower the reported MMRV.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Table 3, grasp and Success columns
evidence.detail: WidowX results distinguish partial grasping from completion. Put Carrot on Plate full success has MMRV 0.111 and r 0.575, despite stronger agreement on some other tasks; rankings are not uniformly perfect.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 5.3 and distribution-shift plot; PDF p. 20, Tables 4–5
evidence.detail: Robustness tests vary background, lighting, distractors, table texture and camera pose for RT-1 with/without augmentation. The plot prints augmented MMRV 0.016, but Table 4 prints 0.041 for the corresponding average. Table 4 uses absolute changes; Table 5 includes variants with improved success.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 5.3, novel distribution shifts; PDF p. 20, Table 6
evidence.detail: For Pick Coke Can, real original/OOD arm-texture success is 0.760/0.520 for RT-1-X and 0.293/0.000 for Octo-Base. Simulated texture ranges are [0.507,0.653] and [0.000,0.293]. Physical arms were changed using gift wrapping paper.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.4, Effect of system identification and adjacent table
evidence.detail: SIMPLER SysID has control loss 0.131 and MMRV 0.031. Perturbed settings give 0.267/0.070 and 0.432/0.100, respectively.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.4, visual-matching ablation table/text; PDF p. 21, Table 7, checkpoint headers and component rows
evidence.detail: The main ablation gives MMRV/success gap 0.087/0.272 with no matching and 0.050/0.136 with all components. Green screen plus drawer matching alone gives MMRV 0.142. Main prose lists RT-1 Begin, while Table 7 labels RT-1 15%; this discrepancy is unresolved.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Table 8(a–b), physical-property ablations
evidence.detail: Can masses 10–80 g and gripper friction coefficients 0.25–2.0 retain MMRV 0.031, with r spanning 0.957–0.990. Drawer joint-friction tests also retain relatively low ranking violations. The experiments concern six Google policies and specified rigid-object tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, simulator comparison; PDF p. 21, Table 9, five-policy Isaac Sim Variant Aggregation results
evidence.detail: Isaac Sim tests cover Pick Coke Can and Move Near with five policies. Table 9 gives MMRV/r 0.064/0.973 and 0.053/0.865 for average success, respectively; absolute success differs from reality.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Appendix F.1, simulation-free comparison and Table 10
evidence.detail: MSE uses 25 Bridge validation trajectories but 25 RT-1 training trajectories because no public RT-1 validation split exists. Correlation uses negative MSE. Table 10 changes drawer values relative to Table 1: MSE 0.346/0.264 and Visual Matching 0.055/0.915 for MMRV/r.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Table 11 and Appendix F.1; PDF p. 23, F.1 continuation
evidence.detail: An added RT-1 policy is trained solely on can-picking demonstrations. Its real/sim success is 0.680/0.403, and the expanded comparison reports MMRV 0.027 and r 0.959.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Table 12 and Appendix F.2
evidence.detail: Kruskal-Wallis tests compare per-policy real and simulated trial-success distributions. Table 12 counts policies with p below 0.05; some tasks have detected shifts despite favorable ranking results.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 23–24, Appendix G, limitations (1)–(5)
evidence.detail: Limitations include rigid-object tasks, fixed-camera green screening, imperfect shadows, manual scene curation, RGB/proprioceptive inputs and simple contact-free identification. Preliminary Gaussian-splatting scenes had geometry/rendering problems. High-speed collisions and dexterous manipulation require stronger calibration.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.1; PDF pp. 15–18, Appendices A–B
evidence.detail: The PDF gives trajectory counts, controller frequencies, solver and asset tools, but no numeric annealing search bounds, complete annealing schedule, absolute episode time limits, pinned software environment or hardware/compute budget for reproducing the pipeline.
